question.leadin: This ruler founded the Achaemenid [ah-KEE-men-id] Empire, which successfully grew by supporting local rulers as satraps and respecting local customs.
question.text: Name this "Great" Persian ruler of the sixth century BCE who ended the Babylonian Captivity.
question.clue: This son of Persis seized the city of Sardis after defeating the Lydian king, Croesus.

swap.leadin: At the Battles of Issus and Gaugamela, Alexander the Great defeated forces from this empire.
swap.text: Name this empire, which was ruled for some periods by Achaemenids, Safavids, and Afshars. Rulers of this empire included Cyrus the Great and Xerxes (ZERK-seez) the Great.
swap.clue: One ruler of this empire famously ordered the ocean to be whipped.

question.leadin: This country's nationalization of a British oil company prompted the CIA-led overthrow of its Prime Minister, Mohammed Mossadegh.
question.text: Name this nation where the Qajar Dynasty once ruled from Tehran.
question.clue: Cyrus Vance resigned after an operation in this country termed "Eagle Claw".

swap.leadin: Answer the following about the role of the pythia in Ancient Greece.
swap.text: The second Persian invasion of Greece was led by this monarch, the son of Darius I. While victorious at Thermopylae, his armies were defeated at Platea after they burned Athens.
swap.clue: This king's forces were decisively defeated at the Battle of Plataea (plut-AY-uh), after which Athens founded the Delian League.

question.leadin: This victor of the battles of Ipsus and Corupedium was succeeded in his highest post by his son Antiochus after his assassination.
question.text: Name this Diadochos who established a namesake empire in the former easternmost satrapies of Alexander the Great.
question.clue: He dispatched the ambassador Megasthenes on expeditions to the east, resulting in the production of theIndika.

swap.leadin: Translations of the Hebrew Bible into this language were known as targum.
swap.text: Name this ancient Semitic language, used as a lingua franca in Mesopotamia and Judea. Jesus Christ spoke this language inscribed on the sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II.
swap.clue: Demons found in the Ginza Rabba were repelled using ceramic bowls with incantations in this language.

question.text: After Roman triumvirate Crassus tried to invade this empire and failed, his was head was cut off and filled with molten gold in reference to his famous wealth.
question.clue: This empire's namesake "shot" consisted of turning around on horseback during retreat to fire at the advancing army.

swap.leadin: Carsten Niebuhr ("NEE-boor") copied a document commissioned by this ruler that shows him looking up at a farvahar.
swap.text: Name this ruler who seized power in a civil war following the assassination of the impostor Gaumata. This commissioner of the Behistun Inscription established the Royal Road to connect his empire from Susa to Sardis.
swap.answerHtml: Darius I (“the first”) [or Darius the Great; prompt on Darius]
swap.clue: Near the end of his life, he ordered a large limestone rock to be inscribed with his genealogy in three languages; that inscription was translated into English in 1849.

question.text: Important to both the Medes and Persians were this priestly class which accomplished feats of prophecy, dream-interpretation, and sorcery later named for them.
question.clue: Darius' rise to power is described in the Bisitun inscription, which claims that Gaumata, one of these people, pretended to be Smerdis, the brother of Cambyses II. These people, who in Sasanian times were led by a chief figure called the mowbed, are described by Herodotus as one of six Median tribes.

swap.text: This Achaemenid public works project linked Susa, a capital in modern-day Iran, to Sardis in Anatolia. It allowed horse-mounted mail couriers to go super-fast.
swap.clue: This was the name given to the ancient highway that connected Susa to Sardis in the Persian Empire. This was also the name given by the Spanish to the more notable parts of the Inca road system.

question.text: Abu Bakr's military endeavors included sending Khalid ibn al-Walid to campaign against this empire. Its last emperor Yazdegerd III was defeated by al-Walid at the Battle of Qadisiyyah.
question.clue: This empire was defeated at Qadisiyyah at the hands of Umar's general, Khalid ibn al-Walid.

swap.leadin: According to legend, a man in this battle died after being struck by a soldier named Mithridates.
swap.text: Name this battle in which Artaxerxes II put down a revolt led by his younger brother, Cyrus the Younger. Cyrus had hired a Greek group of mercenaries known as the Ten Thousand.
swap.clue: Clearchus took command of one side's army after this battle, but was himself later murdered at a banquet given by Tissaphernes.

question.leadin: After the ominous appearance of an eclipse that was accurately predicted by Thales of Miletus, this empire was quick to offer a draw to a rival power, led by Alyattes, at the Battle of Halys River.
question.text: Name this empire whose capital, Ecbatana, supposedly had seven differently-colored walls. This empire's ruler Deioces ("dy-oh-kees") created an early spy ring called "the king's eyes and ears."
question.clue: As a result of a battle at the Halys River, that waterway was declared its border with Lydia.

swap.leadin: A widely rejected theory links the language of this ancient kingdom to South India's Dravidian language family.
swap.text: Name this kingdom in modern Western Iran whose king, Shutruk-Nahhunte, took the stelae ("STEE-lee") of the Babylonian kings Naram-Sin and Hammurabi back to his capital of Susa during a 12th-century BC invasion of the Kassite Dynasty.
swap.clue: The "Lament for Ur" describes a conquest by these people, whose Shutrukid dynasty later defeated the Kassites and looted the stele bearing the Code of Hammurabi from Babylon.

question.leadin: Henry Rawlinson was the first modern European to translate the writing on this document.
question.text: Name this document which Darius ("DARE-ee-us") the Great used to dedicate his victories to the "grace of Ahura Mazda."
question.clue: This monumental inscription, incorrectly ascribed to Semiramis by Ctesias and now in modern day Kermanshah province, is carved in three languages: Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. It celebrates the defeat of nine rebel kings.

swap.text: During his rise to power, Septimius Severus defeated Pescennius Niger at this place in Turkey. In a 333 BC battle at this location, Alexander the Great defeated Darius III, setting up their final clash at Gaugamela.
swap.clue: In addition to that defeat of Pescennius Niger, this was the site of a 1266 battle at which King Hethum I of Armenia was defeated by Baibars.

question.text: An "archaeological complex" named for Bactria and this region was home to Gonur Depe ("go-NOOR deh-PEH"), where Harappan seals have been found. A much later mention of this region's name appears in the Behistun Inscription, which records the rebellion of Frada there.
question.answerHtml: Margiana [or Marguš or Margush or Margiane or Marv; accept Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex; accept Frāda of Margiana]

swap.leadin: George Rawlinson re-read Strabo's claim that these people required that men must have at least five wives as a misinterpretation of a limit on the size of their harems.
swap.text: Heleen Sancisi-Weerdenburg quipped that what people's short-lived empire "exists for us because Herodotus said it did," referencing the historian's questionable accounts of kings like Deioces and Astyages?
swap.clue: Early kings of these people included Deioces and Phraortes.

question.text: This son of Kavahd didn't care much for Mazdak or his sect and ousted them. This ruler is likely the most renowned Sassanid king and warred with Justinian after concluding the Eternal Peace with him. His grandson, the second ruler of his name, was busted up by Heraclius.
question.answerHtml: Chosroes I (or Khosrau or Khusrav or Khosrow or Osroes or Husrev)
question.clue: Justinian's main rival throughout his reign was this Sassanid Emperor, who prosecuted the Lazic War and defeated the Bactrians and the Hephthalite Empire during his rule from 531-579 AD.

swap.leadin: Answer the following about a kingdom in Asia FTPE.
swap.text: Ecbatana was the capital of this kingdom, which was absorbed into Cyrus the Great's budding Persian Empire around 550 B.C.
swap.clue: The city of Nineveh was captured by his successor Cyaxares, who extended this kingdom's borders to the Halys river in Asia Minor.
